title: Broad Peak Avalanche Kills Four, Nirmal Purja Among Six Still Missing
excerpt: A devastating avalanche on Pakistan's 12th-highest peak swept away 10 climbers from four expeditions, including American Mallory Geis who had left her Pilates career to pursue mountaineering.
body:
• An avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak (8,051m) on July 30 struck 10 climbers between Camp 2 and Camp 3; four bodies have been recovered, six remain missing
  • Among the dead is Sarah Mallory Geis, 39, a San Antonio woman who closed her Pilates studio this year to pursue high-altitude mountaineering
  • Famed Nepali climber Nirmal "Nims" Purja, star of the Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, remains unaccounted for as rescue operations resume Saturday

An avalanche tore through Pakistan's Broad Peak on Thursday, killing at least four climbers and leaving six others missing, including renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal "Nims" Purja, in one of the deadliest incidents on the Karakoram peak in decades.

Among the confirmed dead is Sarah Mallory Geis, a 39-year-old American from San Antonio, Texas, who earlier this year closed her Pilates studio to pursue her mountaineering ambitions full-time. "Taking a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes," she had written on Instagram in February. This was her first attempt at an 8,000-meter summit.

What Happened on the Mountain

The avalanche struck around 9:20 a.m. local time on July 30, catching climbers between Camp 2 and Camp 3 at an altitude between 6,450 and 7,000 meters, according to Naila Kiani of the Alpine Club of Pakistan. Four separate expeditions were on the mountain at the time: an Elite Exped team led by Purja, an Imagine Nepal expedition, a Seven Summit Treks group, and a team consisting of Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi and Geis.

"Their tracking beacon data show they were thrown hundreds of meters down the mountain. The bodies of two climbers and the severed leg of a third were later found near base camp, highlighting the avalanche's brutal force."

— Naila Kiani, Alpine Club of Pakistan

In total, 10 climbers were on the affected section of the route: six Nepalese nationals, one American, one Chinese, one Omani, and one Pakistani. The 10 had lost all communication with base camp following the avalanche, said Karrar Haidri, vice president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

Rescue crews recovered four bodies on Friday, identifying three as Geis; Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy of Oman; and Pur Bahadur Gurung of Nepal. The identity of the fourth victim has not been publicly announced. Drone footage showed signs of additional bodies in the search area, according to the Gilgit-Baltistan regional government.

A Career Abandoned for the Mountains

Geis had worked alongside her father, George, in the family's real-estate business before running her Pilates studio. She served as a board member of San Antonio Sports, a group that brings major sporting events to the city. "The impact she made in our community will never be forgotten," the organization said in a statement.

Before the expedition, she had written on social media: "I'm heading out for my first big kid climbing expedition in Pakistan. Let's see if we can get this body and these boots up Broad Peak, the 12th highest mountain in the world."

Local mountaineer Mirza Ali, who met the teams at base camp, recalled Geis's warmth. "When our team got back from the summit, Sohail and Mallory welcomed us at base camp. They applauded our return and served us coffee," he told Le Monde. "Mallory was full of life."

Purja's Legacy Hangs in the Balance

Purja, 43, became a global figure after setting the record for the fastest ascent of all 14 of the world's 8,000-meter peaks, completing the feat in just 189 days in 2019. His journey was chronicled in the 2021 Netflix documentary 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. A former British Special Forces soldier of Nepali origin, he had arrived at Broad Peak's base camp just days before the disaster.

His business partner, Mingma David Sherpa, told Nepali outlet Kantipur that Purja's tracking device showed some activity on Friday morning, though it remained unclear whether the movement indicated activity from Purja himself. Mingma David said he was traveling to Pakistan after hearing the news.

"We hope to continue our operations, both aerial search and the ground rescue, till the time we find the survivors or the dead bodies."

— Irfan Arshad, President, Alpine Club of Pakistan

What's Next

Rescue operations were suspended Friday night due to poor weather that prevented helicopter flights, said Faisal Ehsan Pirzada, the interior minister for Gilgit-Baltistan. Two Pakistan Army Aviation helicopters have been dispatched, and search efforts are expected to resume Saturday.

The area where the avalanche struck had not previously been considered particularly dangerous. "This is the first time we've heard of such a large avalanche there," said Ali, the local mountaineer. Since Broad Peak was first climbed in 1957, at least 39 climbers have died on its slopes, according to the Alpine Club of Pakistan.

Nepal's foreign ministry said it had received assurances from Pakistani authorities that all available resources would be mobilized for search and rescue. China said it was "urgently verifying the situation" regarding its nationals. Geis's father, George, told CNN affiliate KENS that the family's focus is now on bringing his daughter home. "Well, it's tough. It's tough," he said. "Our main objective now is to get her back here."
nri_angle: The avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, in the Karakoram range of Gilgit-Baltistan, killed Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi and disrupted a region central to Pakistan's growing mountaineering tourism industry.
author: Diaspora Desk
